sn56.30:1.1: The Cetīs were a rather obscure people living in the Bundelkhand division of Madhya Pradesh, south of Vaccha and west of Magadha, around the Vettavatī river (Sanskrit vetravatī, modern Betwa), a tributary of the Yamunā flowing from the Vindhya ranges to the south. Apart from this Sutta, three discourses feature Mahācunda there (AN 6.46, AN 10.24, AN 10.85). A century after the Buddha, Revata stopped there heading south from Saṅkassa, where ten leading monks met him to discuss the dispute at the upcoming Second Council (Kd 22:1.9.39). | The spelling of the city is highly uncertain: sayaṁjāti, sahajāti, sañjāti, sahañcanika, sahajaniya. The commentary to Ja 422 says the name of the Cetī capital was Sotthivatī, sometimes identified with Śuktimatī found in Sanskrit sources. Possibly these variants reflect attempts to render the local dialect. The sense of the name is “one’s own caste”, perhaps suggesting they were an insular people.
sn56.30:2.1: Gavampati (“lord of cows”) appears in DN 23:33.1, where he is said to spend his days meditating in a celestial palace. That Sutta, like the present one, does not speak of the Buddha as still living, although the current Sutta asserts that he heard this teaching from the Buddha. He also has a single verse at Thag 1.38, where he is said to have stilled the mighty Sarabhū river with his powers. Gavampati was also said to have been among the friends of Yasa who were among the earliest ordained monks (Kd 1:9.1.1). The Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya says that he was invited to the First Council after the Buddha’s passing, but declined as his own time was drawing near. These passages, slight as they are, suggest a somewhat mystical figure, whose legend perhaps grew due to his reclusive nature. In later years he came to be regarded as one of the 80 great disciples, and he remains an object of worship in South-east Asia. | Read there bhikkhū. | This passage is cited at Kv 2.9:26.3.
